title: Testing Data with dbt & Great Expectations

scenes.line1: How do you automate data checks?
scenes.say: How do you make sure your data is clean before it hits production? Which tools help you catch problems early in the pipeline?

scenes.label: Schema
scenes.sub: dbt tests things like uniqueness or nulls at the model level.
scenes.say: With dbt, you can test your data models for things like unique values or missing data. It works right at the schema level.

scenes.code:
models:
  - name: customers
    tests:
      - unique:
          column_name: customer_id
scenes.say: For example, you can set up a test to make sure every customer ID is unique in your customers table.

scenes.label: Granular
scenes.sub: Great Expectations validates data with custom or built-in checks.
scenes.say: Great Expectations lets you define more detailed checks, like making sure every row meets certain rules.
You might use an expectation to check that customer IDs are unique, right down to individual rows.
I use dbt for big picture, schema-level tests, and Great Expectations for more detailed, row-level checks.

scenes.question: Should you use dbt for row-level checks?
scenes.wrong: Yes, dbt handles all row checks.
scenes.right: No, dbt focuses on schema tests. Use Great Expectations for row-level validation.
scenes.say: Here's a common mix-up: should you use dbt for row-level checks? Actually, dbt is best for schema tests. For row-level validation, go with Great Expectations.
